difficultyRationale: Checks understanding of the mechanism auto-configuration classes actually use to stay out of the way of user-defined beans, not just the fact that they do.
prompt: A Spring Boot starter's auto-configuration class declares a `JavaMailSender` bean annotated `@ConditionalOnMissingBean(JavaMailSender.class)`. A developer defines their own `@Bean` of type `JavaMailSender` in their application's configuration. Why does the application end up using the developer's bean rather than the starter's?
explanation: `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` makes the annotated bean definition's registration conditional on no bean of the given type already existing in the application context at the point the condition is evaluated. Auto-configuration classes are processed after the user's own `@Configuration` classes in the ordering Spring Boot uses, so by the time the starter's `JavaMailSender` definition is evaluated, the developer's own bean is already registered — the condition is false, the starter's bean is skipped, and only the developer's bean exists.

options.text: Spring always prefers a `@Bean` method defined in the application's own package over one originating from a dependency's auto-configuration class, regardless of any `@Conditional*` annotations attached to either bean definition.
options.explanation: There is no package-based precedence rule in Spring's bean resolution; the actual mechanism here is the `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` condition evaluating false because a bean of that type already exists.

options.text: `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` skips the starter's registration once a bean of that type exists; user config runs before auto-configuration, so the developer's bean is already there when checked.
options.explanation: Correct — this is exactly the back-off mechanism auto-configuration classes use: they are ordered to run after the user's own configuration, and `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` lets them defer to whatever the user already defined.

options.text: Both the starter's bean and the developer's bean are registered in the context, and Spring resolves the ambiguity at injection time by applying `@Primary` semantics automatically to whichever bean the developer defined.
options.explanation: No second `JavaMailSender` bean is registered at all in this case — `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` prevents the starter's bean definition from being created in the first place, so there is no `@Primary`-style disambiguation happening between two beans.

options.text: This only works because the developer also added `@Primary` to their bean definition; without that annotation, both beans would be registered side by side and startup would fail outright with an ambiguous-bean resolution error.
options.explanation: `@Primary` is unnecessary here because the starter's bean is never registered in the first place; the described outcome follows directly from `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`'s ordering, with no ambiguity to resolve.
